newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia criticises Croatia over embassy security.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia criticises Croatia over embassy security.

text.p: The Bosnian ambassador to Croatia accused the Zagreb government of failing to provide adequate security for his embassy at a time of strained relations between the two countries, Bosnian television reported on Tuesday.
Ambassador Kasim Trnka told Bosnian state television that "Croatian police called off 24-hour guard duty in front of the Bosnian embassy" and other embassies in the capital Zagreb.

Trnka said his government had conveyed its dissatisfaction to Croatian authorities over the move and said Sarajevo had "reminded" Croatia that international law obliged a host-country to provide security for diplomatic missions.
"We expect a response from the Croatian side and warned them that we are not satisfied with reduced security measures," Trnka said by telephone.
Trnka was also quoted as saying that the embassy had received some threats by telephone from anonymous callers.

A Croatian official with state protocol told Bosnian television that the decision to scale back 24-hour guard duty was based on a judgment that the security situation in Zagreb had changed and "should be interpreted like this".
The official said the Croatian government was not obligated to post armed guards outside embassies.
The dispute over embassy security coincides with a rise in tensions in Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation sparked by violence in the southern town of Mostar this month.

The NATO-led peace force has stepped up patrols and conducted searches for unauthorised weapons in Mostar after armed Croat men attacked a procession of Moslems trying to visit a cemetery in the Croat-held western quarter this month.
International police monitors are investigating the incident and are expected to announce the results of their findings this week.

Diplomats have appealed to the Croatian government to exert influence over their Bosnian Croat proteges who have been blamed for obstructing international efforts to reunify the divided town of Mostar.
Bosnian Moslems and Croats fought a vicious 10-month war in 1993-94 before agreeing to form the federation under heavy U.S. pressure.
Croat nationalists accuse Bosnian Moslem authorities of failing to protect the rights of the Croat minority in the federation, which together with a Serb republic comprises peacetime Bosnia.
